 “The Wonka of Worcester” Director Justin O’Neill Discusses Death, AI and Chocolate 
 By Elijah Fischer 
 November 16, 2026 
 Image Credit: Image Courtesy of Justin O’Niell
 “I think about death a lot,” 24-year-old filmmaker Justin O’Neill tells me. “How do you prevail in a world that’s forgotten about you?” 
 Hidden in Justin’s neighborhood in Montgomery County, PA, is Bergin’s Chocolate, a 91-year-old candy company that specializes in handcrafted chocolates. The business is family owned, and most of the machinery used to run it has been passed down across the decades from owner to owner. 
 “One owner told me that they don’t make parts for these machines anymore. So if they break, that’s just it.” O’Niell said. “I thought that was incredibly interesting that these people still show up and do things the patient way, knowing intuitively that maybe this won’t last.” 
 Bergin’s Chocolate and the family who run it are the subject of “The Wonka of Worcester,” a silent documentary short O’Niell shot on 16-mm film. Without the use of any speech or voice over, O’Niell documents the work of Begin’s owners through verite style footage of the chocolate making process. One shot follows a single piece through a fiery conveyor belt, another marks the symmetry as each chocolate is meticulously hand-cut. As the family work, outside the sun shrinks over suburban Pennsylvania, painting a portrait of purgatory O’Niell aimed to capture with an “anti-AI” tint. 
 “[Shooting on 16-mm] was so important to me because it’s a fragile process, very much like the chocolate making.” O’Neill said. Initially he wanted to shoot the film like a standard documentary, but shortly before filming he decided to tackle things with a different approach. “I didn’t want to just shoot things like [they were] news coverage,” he said. “I wanted to focus on the in-between moments.” 
 O’Neill’s unique approach and kinetic visualization earned him an honorable mention for Most Innovative Short at the 35th Philadelphia Film Festival. He said, “There were times [during shooting] where I would be like ‘Hey, when you’re looking at this chocolate, do you mind thinking of your Mom?’ It’s small things like that [which make the movie], something for [the subjects] to go off of.” 
 Though filming only took 3 days, production on the short from first rumblings to final edit took months. “I like to really live with an edit,” O’Niell said. “I don’t want to play it safe.” 
 When asked why shoot on film, he said, “I think it forces you to consider all aspects, because you either get the shot you want or you’re wasting stuff. I feel like for ‘Wonka,’ especially for something as simple as the silhouette shots, you have to consider the sun, the cars outside, the tools on the ground.” 
 He also emphasized the importance of having to physically look through the camera as you shoot. “Looking through the frame when you see it and no one else sees it, it’s an intimate thing you share with your DP,” he explains. “I think it makes you a better filmmaker.” 
 “The Wonka of Worcester” is a film with visuals that are firmly rooted in setting suns and liminality, something O’Niell says is far from an accident. “I firmly believe there’s a death to childhood,” he said. O’Niell grew up sharing a neighborhood with Bergin’s Chocolates, a proximity that drew him to the subject in the first place. 
 “My great grandfather was very happy I was doing filmmaking, but he once told me ‘You’re gonna get older and you’re not gonna want to do it anymore. That’s just what happens when you get older, the things you loved and the things you were passionate about, they just kind of dissipate.’ And that scared me for a long time, but I think that’s why seeing someone as old as Mike [one of the owners of Bergin’s Chocolates] being passionate, and believing in something he’s done his whole life was so enticing to me” he shared.  
 “The song we use is in the film is called ‘Who Knows Where The Time Goes?’ by Sandy Denny.” O’Niell said, a choice motivated by the many spinning cogs of Bergin’s that resemble clockwork. 
 “We didn’t record any live sound,” he revealed. O’Niell employed sound designers to instead capture the feeling of the factory through foley. “A lot of the sound design is actually clocks,” he said. “I wanted to express that feeling of mortality and time running out not only visually, but sonically too.” 
 The short is currently continuing to forge a path on the festival circuit, with no current plans for online or widespread distribution.“I hate the idea of putting something [on YouTube]  and it just lives and dies there,” he said. “I definitely want to make this film more than that, but I’m still navigating what that is.”  
 “The Wonka of Worcester” is undeniably singular as a documentary short. It isn’t difficult to see why O’Niell was noted for his innovation: From placing fragile film cameras in precarious situations to get the perfect shot, to capturing melancholic nostalgia through the morning light, his vision is what sets his short apart from more standard documentaries. Even without distribution, it’s clear that like Bergin’s, Justin O’Niell and “The Wonka of Worcester” will be persevering in the name of passion. 
 Elijah Fischer is a senior majoring in English with minors in Journalism and Film Criticism. AF997636@wcupa.edu.
